newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Savings Bank upbeat on restructuring move.
newsitem.headline: Albania Savings Bank upbeat on restructuring move.

text.p: Albania's state-owned Savings Bank said on Wednesday it was confident it would be able to cope with the burden of incorporating parts of two state banks, which are destined for privatisation within two years.

General manager Bedri Collaku said the Savings Bank (SBA) would take on 22 branches of the National Commercial Bank (NCBA) and 23 branches of the Rural Commercial Bank (RCBA) by the end of March 1997.
The move meant its loan portfolio would increase by 50 percent to 64 billion leks ($640 million) and deposits and current accounts would rise by 30 percent, he added.
"This process will increase the value of the bank and you will see its reputation grow further although we are taking some burdens from the other banks," Collaku said.
The transfer of NCBA and RCBA branches to the Savings Bank is part of a two-stage restructuring programme which aims to turn all three banks into private hands by the year 2000.
Albania in 1992 created a two-tier banking system with the Bank of Albania serving as a central institution to the state-owned NCBA, RCBA and SBA.
Collaku, also a ruling Democratic Party deputy, said a recent privatisation law aimed at restructuring banks should make them more attractive to potential strategic investors.
"The first measure was to restructure the network so the most important branches (in eight key regions) remained an integral part of the other banks," Collaku said.
The bank had witnessed an influx of around $800,000 in hard currency into the bank in one day last week, a trend which had begun in mid-December and was growing increasingly visible.
"Depositors are receiving payments from firms (operating get-rich-quick schemes), turning them into dollars and trusting them to us. This has influenced the market," he added.
The dollar rose by 3.5 points against the lek on Monday to 108 leks. It closed at 108.5 leks on Thursday.

Alleged pyramid schemes offering high interest have drawn millions of dollars from depositors in Albania over the past year, taking money away from the banks. One of the schemes has collapsed and two have temporarily stopped paying depositors.
"But people are turning back to the banks and what striking is our hard currency deposits are growing," he added. ($1=108 leks)
